hpi:
{{patient_name}} presents with classic trigeminal neuralgia — recurrent episodes of severe, sharp, electric shock-like facial pain in one area of the trigeminal nerve distribution, lasting seconds to two minutes, often precipitated by innocuous stimuli (light touch, chewing, wind). The most common cause is compression of the trigeminal nerve root (80–90% of cases), typically by a vascular loop.

Differential: acute herpes zoster, painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, idiopathic painful trigeminal neuropathy, postherpetic trigeminal neuropathy.

Workup: neurologic exam including cranial nerves; CBC to exclude infection; BMP/CMP; MRI or CT head to exclude tumor or neurovascular compression.

First-line treatment is carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; gabapentin/pregabalin are second line. Surgery is not indicated until medical therapy fails.

case_summary:
Differential: Acute herpes zoster, Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, Idiopathic painful trigeminal neuropathy, postherpetic trigeminal neuropathy.

The patient has classic Trigeminal neuralgia. The most common cause of trigeminal neuralgia is compression of the trigeminal nerve root (80-90% of cases). The compression is typically caused by a vascular loop.

The criteria to diagnose trigeminal neuralgia include: having recurrent episodes of facial pain in one area of the trigeminal nerve; pain lasting seconds to 2 minutes; severe intensity; sharp/electric pain which can be precipitated by innocuous stimuli within the affected trigeminal distribution.

MRI/CT scan should be done to rule out lesions such as tumor or neurovascular compression. The first line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia is Carbamazepine or Oxcarbazepine. Gabapentin can also be used, but this is second line. Surgery does not need to be consulted as medical treatment should occur and fail prior to involving surgery.
